en.html:
So that was that.

By yesterday evening, we had somehow finished the bridge's foundations. Not a handsome job, but finished. This morning, a beaver's lodge stood in their place. The collapse was so complete that nobody looking at it would suspect we had ever intended a bridge.

One look gave the likely reason. The river had risen in the rain; our work had apparently not been equal to this small disagreement.

en.html:
My fellow builders stared down at the wreckage without a word. Even for speaking, they seemed to have no energy left.

My own condition was not very different.

We stood in a row like stone Jizo statues while the neighbors passed behind us. Now and then, somebody made sure we received a laugh at our expense.

...We had been too optimistic.

The biggest mistake was probably that the foundation piles were too shallow. We had considered the soft riverbed and driven them deep—or what we had generously decided was deep. It had not been enough.

Other faults came to mind also. Most were things we had noticed while working, then collectively settled with 'probably all right.' Such excellent agreement we had achieved over our mistakes.

We should have taken more care...

en.html:
No answer. Only that heavy sense of wasted effort coming out with their breath.

I could hardly blame them. Yes, we had accepted that the work might achieve nothing. Seeing it actually, completely achieve nothing was a different matter. Who would not lose heart?

I could not think of a way to encourage them, either.

...For now, at least, recover the wreckage.

I stepped into the river and took hold of the timber. It had gone into avant-garde art without consulting us.

Kageaki"Yes."
Old Man"All of you are complete amateurs, correct?"
Kageaki"Yes... None of us has built a bridge before."
Old Man"Not even one carpenter among the whole lot."
Kageaki"Your assessment is correct."

Old Man"I'm retired now. Used to be a carpenter. Built a few bridges also."
Old Man"A house stands on ground that stays put. A bridge has to get along with a river that keeps moving. Much more trouble, that."
Kageaki"...I see."

en.html:
This, I had not expected.

The established residents and the newly arrived refugees were working side by side. Helping each other to build one thing.

Not that they had made peace. Let me not give myself that much credit.

They exchanged no words and no smiles. When their eyes met, the looks were cold. Their distrust was still very much present.

Even so.

When heavy timber had to be carried.
When piles had to be driven into the riverbed.

One man would help another with work too much for a single pair of hands. And sometimes, one was a resident and the other a refugee.

ja.html:
予想せぬ光景だった。

　旧来の住民と新参の難民が、共に立ち働いている。
　一つのものを造るため――協力して。

　彼らは和解してはいない。

　言葉を交わす事はなく、笑顔を向け合う事もない。
　時折交差する視線は冷たく、相手への不信感を隠し
切れていない。

　それでも。
　
　――重い材木を担ぎ出す時。
　――川底へ杭を打ち込む時。

　一人では手に余る作業を、別の一人が手伝い、その
両者が住民同士でも難民同士でもない事がある。

Kageaki"Would a width sufficient for one person be all right?"
Old Man"A little more. Enough for two people to pass... then a cart can use it also."
Kageaki"That would certainly help. But the materials may not be enough."
Old Man"Don't worry about that. If it comes to it, I'll speak to my old workplace."
Kageaki"...I am putting you to a great deal of trouble."
Old Man"Heh."
